Use this whenever the user mentions gRPC, proto/protobuf, plugin methods, the gRPC bridge, tonic, reflection descriptors, 'missing plugins' in the gRPC diagnostic page, or the seal/freeze/hot pipeline — even if they don't say 'gRPC' explicitly (e.g. 'the plugin isn't showing up on the diagnostic page', 'add a method to plugin X', 'regen protos')."

8|
9|# gRPC Expert — OP-DBUS
10|
11|This workspace does **not** hand-write per-plugin `.proto` files. Proto generation is
12|automatic, driven entirely by each plugin's `PluginSchema`. If you remember one thing
13|from this skill: **fixing a plugin's gRPC surface means editing its Rust schema
14|function, not writing `.proto`.**
15|
16|## The real pipeline (roll → seal → freeze → hot)
17|
18|```
19|1. Plugin declares  → PluginSchema { methods: HashMap<String, MethodDecl>, signals: Vec<SignalDecl>, ... }
20|                       in crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<plugin>.rs
21|2. Schema gets put   → op-projection's SchemaEngine publishes the catalog hash
22|                       (op_identity::schema_bridge::schema_catalog_hash())
23|3. Sealed by blob    → op-blob seals the plugin object into an immutable blob:
24|                       /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob
25|                       (op-blob is the ONLY writer — never write blobs elsewhere)
26|4. Descriptors       → TWO separate reflection layers exist, don't confuse them:
27|   for reflection       a) STATIC: crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs generates
28|                            plugin_methods.proto from every plugin's schema.methods,
29|                            compiles it with tonic_build into operation_descriptor.bin
30|                            (a protobuf FileDescriptorSet), served by tonic-reflection.
31|                         b) DYNAMIC: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/dynamic_reflection.rs
32|                            (ActiveReflectionCatalog) hydrates live from the sealed
33|                            SHM blob catalog via hydrate_reflection_from_shm() —
34|                            this is the "frozen" descriptor set for what's actually
35|                            present right now, independent of what's compiled in.
36|5. Frozen            → the blob + its descriptors are immutable once sealed.
37|6. gRPC socket = hot → crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs registers the
38|                       generated per-plugin service (plugin_method_routes.rs,
39|                       add_routes()) on the tonic UDS bridge, dispatching each
40|                       RPC to call_generated_plugin_method_typed(plugin_id,
41|                       schema_name, ...) which routes through PluginService.CallMethod
42|                       — i.e. gRPC never bypasses D-Bus, it's a bridge, not a
43|                       second control plane.
44|```
45|
46|A plugin shows green/connected on the gRPC diagnostic page **iff**:
47|- its `PluginSchema.methods` is non-empty (empty → `build.rs` silently skips it —
48|  see `collect_plugin_methods()`), **and**
49|- the plugin is sealed in the SHM blob catalog.
50|
51|These are discovery prerequisites, not proof of execution. Canonical dispatch
52|also requires the method's complete declaration and plugin version to match the
53|compiled handler, argument validation, verified identity, and its exact grant.
54|An advertised method whose adapter is absent is unfinished work.
55|
56|## Where to actually make changes
57|
58|| Task | File |
59||---|---|
60|| Add/fix methods for plugin `<name>` | `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs`, inside `<name>_schema()` |
61|| Reusable input/output builders | `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs` |
62|| Regenerate the derived `.proto` + routes | Just rebuild — `build.rs` regenerates on every `cargo build -p op-grpc-bridge` (it `rerun-if-changed`s `../op-plugins/src/state_plugins`) |
63|| Wire a genuinely new (non-plugin-derived) service | `crates/op-grpc-bridge/proto/*.proto`, add to the `compile_protos` list + `rerun-if-changed` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs`, then register in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs` |
64|| Inspect what's currently generated | `target/{debug,release}/build/op-grpc-bridge-*/out/plugin_methods.proto` (build artifact — never hand-edit) |
65|
66|**Never** create files under a `/proto/plugin_methods/` directory or a
67|`plugin_methods_unified.proto` by hand — those paths don't exist in this repo and
68|aren't part of the real pipeline; that was a stale spec from an earlier session.
69|The single source of truth is `schema.methods`.
70|
71|## Adding methods to a plugin (the actual workflow)
72|
73|Look at `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/proxy_server.rs` (`proxy_server_schema()`)
74|for the canonical pattern:
75|
76|```rust
77|use op_state_store::{MethodDecl, PluginSchema, SideEffect};
78|
79|schema.methods.insert(
80|    "start_proxy".to_string(),
81|    method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<StartProxyInput, plugin_scaffold_helpers::AckOutput>(
82|        "start_proxy",
83|        SideEffect::Mutation,       // Read | Mutation
84|        false,                       // idempotent?
85|        "cap.network.proxy.start@v1",   // required_capability
86|        "mut.network.proxy.start@v1",   // subid — must follow the taxonomy in CLAUDE.md
87|    ),
88|);
89|```
90|
91|- Define `StartProxyInput` (and a typed output struct, or reuse `AckOutput`) as
92|  `#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)]` structs — the JSON Schema is derived, never
93|  hand-written as `serde_json::json!({...})` unless there's no existing helper.
94|- `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<Input, Output>` is the current
95|  (non-deprecated) helper; the single-generic `method_decl_from_schemars` is
96|  deprecated but still present for legacy callers.
97|- `subid` must be registered in the canonical registry per CLAUDE.md
98|  (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/oscal_subid_registry.rs`) — CI enforces
99|  uniqueness.
100|- For plugins with **zero** declared methods today (the ones missing from the
101|  diagnostic page), don't hand-author their methods one by one — see
102|  **The Auto-Creator Plugin** below. That's the actual deliverable: a plugin
103|  that finds these gaps and fills them itself, using real research per plugin.
104|
105|## The Auto-Creator Plugin (an ongoing capability, not a one-off batch)
106|
107|This is **not** a one-time task to fix ~11 named plugins. It's a standing
108|system capability: whenever the system encounters *any* missing plugin —
109|now, or a new one added in the future — it automatically generates that
110|plugin and submits it for **human review**, never auto-merges/auto-seals it
111|unreviewed. The current ~11 gaps are just the first real instances that
112|exercise this, not the scope.
113|
114|Consistent with this workspace's "reactive, not polled" principle (CLAUDE.md):
115|this should be triggered by an actual arrival/lookup that reveals the gap
116|(e.g. a D-Bus/gRPC call or reflection lookup against a plugin whose
117|`schema.methods` is empty, or a plugin name that doesn't resolve at all),
118|not a cron-style sweep re-scanning all plugins on a timer.
119|
120|Build it as a plugin itself (same `PluginSchema`/`MethodDecl` pattern as every
121|plugin in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`), whose job is to:
122|
123|1. **Detect a gap on encounter** — when something references a plugin that's
124|   missing or has `schema.methods.is_empty()` (same emptiness check
125|   `build.rs::collect_plugin_methods` already uses to skip plugins), that's
126|   the trigger — not a periodic scan of the whole registry.
127|2. **Research that specific gap** — drive deep research via the **NotebookLM
128|   MCP** (once wired up) to determine what capabilities/operations the
129|   missing plugin should realistically expose, given its existing state
130|   struct (if any), documentation, and prior art from comparable plugins
131|   already in the registry. This replaces guessing or generic Get/List/Watch
132|   stubs with a grounded, plugin-specific proposal.
133|3. **Synthesize typed schemas** — turn the research output into real Rust
134|   input/output structs (`#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)]`) and `MethodDecl`
135|   entries — per the "no `AckOutput`" rule above, every synthesized method
136|   needs its own meaningful typed request/response, not a generic ack.
137|4. **Submit for human review — do not auto-apply.** The output is a proposed
138|   plugin/schema (e.g. a diff/PR against `<name>_schema()`, or a new
139|   `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs` for a wholly new plugin),
140|   held for a human to approve before it's merged. Only after human approval
141|   does it enter the normal pipeline (build → proto → reflection → sealed
142|   blob → hot). The auto-creator must never seal a blob or register a plugin
143|   into the live catalog on its own. It never emits `.proto` directly and
144|   never writes to `/proto/plugin_methods/` — the single source of truth
145|   stays `schema.methods`, authored by a human-approved change.
146|
147|In short: this is a **standing, reactive meta-plugin that drafts schemas for
148|whatever plugin is found missing, research-backed via NotebookLM, gated by
149|human review** — not a fixed batch job for a specific list of plugins.
150|
151|## JSON Schema → proto mapping
152|
153|The shared mapper lives in `crates/op-blob/src/json_schema_proto.rs`; the bridge
154|uses it for generated native messages. Structured objects become typed nested
155|messages; typed string-key maps retain their value types. Scalars preserve
156|presence, including explicit false, zero and empty strings. Unsigned 64-bit
157|contracts use `uint64`. Nulls, arbitrary JSON, unions and nested arrays use the
158|appropriate standard `Value`/`Struct`/`ListValue` dependencies. Arbitrary numbers
159|inside `Value` remain subject to protobuf's double-precision limit.
160|
161|Two existing wire layouts have distinct numbering rules: generated native
162|bridge fields use stable FNV-1a numbers; sealed per-method messages retain their
163|sorted sequential numbering. Preserve both layouts. Canonical schema map keys
164|and declared transport method names are separate identities, not interchangeable
165|aliases. Consumers register the original sealed descriptors and never reseal,
166|regenerate, or hash them as an existence check.
167|
168|## Known project-specific tensions vs. generic gRPC best practice
169|
170|Be aware of these before applying textbook advice unmodified:
171|
172|- **Do not use `AckOutput { success: bool }` for new/generated methods.**
173|  It exists in the codebase (see `proxy_server.rs`) as a legacy shortcut for
174|  "no meaningful return value," but every method a plugin exposes should have
175|  a real, dedicated typed **input** struct and typed **output** struct that
176|  reflect what the operation actually consumes and returns — not a generic
177|  bool. This matters especially for the auto-creator (below): when it
178|  synthesizes methods for a previously-empty plugin, it must generate a
179|  specific `<Method>Input` and `<Method>Output` schemars struct per method,
180|  never fall back to `AckOutput`. Errors still go through `tonic::Status` /
181|  D-Bus error replies, never a `success: false` field.
182|- **Enums are flattened to `string`, not real proto `enum`.** JSON Schema
183|  `enum` currently maps to proto `string` (see table above), so the classic
184|  `FOO_STATUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0` convention isn't applied by the generator today.
185|  If asked to add real proto enums, that requires changing
186|  `json_schema_type_to_proto` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs`, not just the
187|  plugin schema.
188|- **Streaming comes from state in SHM.** The owner reaffirmed this on
189|  2026-09-13. Methods update authoritative SHM state before notifications;
190|  existing state subscriptions read that state. Current generated method RPCs
191|  being unary does not require another streaming method/service. Preserve
192|  private principal/session scope. Method arguments, event payloads and
193|  generator buffers are not independent state authorities, and buffered unary
194|  responses are not a substitute for SHM state streaming.
195|- **One generated file per bridge crate**, not the "1-1-1" file-per-message
196|  convention — `plugin_methods.proto` bundles every plugin's messages/services
197|  in one generated file. That's fine; it's a build artifact, not hand-maintained
198|  source, so the usual "small modular .proto files" guidance doesn't apply to it.
199|
200|## Generic protobuf/gRPC conventions (still apply to hand-written `.proto`)
201|
202|For any `.proto` you *do* hand-write (domain services under
203|`crates/op-grpc-bridge/proto/`, not plugin-derived ones):
204|
205|- `snake_case` field names, `CamelCase` message/service/RPC names, package names
206|  lowercase (this repo uses `operation.plugin.v1`-style packages).
207|- Reserve field numbers for removed fields; never reuse them.
208|- Prefer `optional` for fields that may be absent; avoid letting one field's
209|  value change the semantic meaning of another.
210|- Real proto `enum`s (where you control the generator, e.g. hand-written
211|  services) always start with `..._UNSPECIFIED = 0`.
212|- Use gRPC status codes (`tonic::Status`) for error paths; reserve response
213|  message fields for actual data.
214|- TLS is mandatory in this workspace (per CLAUDE.md zero-trust transport) —
215|  never wire a new gRPC service as plaintext, even over UDS.
216|- Server reflection (`tonic-reflection`) must stay wired for every new service
217|  so it's discoverable by `op-cognitive-mcp` and the gRPC diagnostic page —
218|  don't add a service that bypasses reflection registration.
219|
220|## Quick diagnostic checklist
221|
222|If a plugin isn't showing up / isn't callable over gRPC:
223|
224|1. Does `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs`'s `<name>_schema()`
225|   actually populate `schema.methods`? (Empty → `build.rs` skips it entirely.)
226|2. Is the plugin registered via `inventory::submit! { PluginReg::new(...) }` in
227|   its own file (self-registration — check `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`
228|   only if the plugin doesn't show up in `available_plugins()` at all)?
229|3. Did `cargo build -p op-grpc-bridge` actually rerun? (`build.rs` only reruns on
230|   changes under `../op-plugins/src/state_plugins` or `build.rs` itself.)
231|4. Is the plugin actually **sealed** in the SHM blob catalog
232|   (`/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/`)? Static compiled-in proto support and the
233|   *dynamic* "hot" reflection/routing are two different gates — a plugin can

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## The Feedback Loop Rule

The feedback loop is the debugging work. Before reading code to build a theory, create or identify a **tight** command that can go red on the user's exact symptom and green when the bug is fixed. A tight loop is fast, deterministic, agent-runnable, and specific enough to catch this bug — not merely "doesn't crash".

When a clean repro is hard, spend disproportionate effort building the loop. Guessing without a red-capable loop is the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Someone wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

---

## Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

### 1. Read Error Messages Carefully

- Don't skip past errors or warnings
- They often contain the exact solution
- Read stack traces completely
- Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

**Action:** Use `read_file` on the relevant source files. Use `search_files` to find the error string in the codebase.

### 2. Build a Tight Feedback Loop

- Can you trigger the user's exact symptom with one command?
- Does the command fail for this bug and only pass once the bug is fixed?
- Is it fast enough to run repeatedly?
- Is it deterministic? For flaky bugs, can you raise the reproduction rate high enough to debug?
- If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess.

**Ways to construct a loop — try in roughly this order:**

1. **Failing test** at the seam that reaches the bug: unit, integration, or end-to-end.
2. **HTTP script / curl** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with fixture input, diffing stdout/stderr against expected output.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright/Puppeteer) asserting on DOM, console, or network.
5. **Replay a captured trace**: HAR, request payload, event log, queue message, or webhook body.
6. **Throwaway harness** that boots the smallest useful slice of the system and calls the failing path.
7. **Property / fuzz loop** when the bug is intermittent wrong output over a broad input space.
8. **Bisection harness** suitable for `git bisect run` when the bug appeared between two known states.
9. **Differential loop** comparing old vs new version, two configs, two providers, or two datasets.
10. **Human-in-the-loop script** only as a last resort: script the human steps and capture their result so the loop stays structured.

**Tighten the loop once it exists:**

- Make it faster: cache setup, narrow scope, skip unrelated initialization.
- Make the signal sharper: assert the exact symptom, not generic success.
- Make it more deterministic: pin time, seed randomness, isolate filesystem, freeze network.

For non-deterministic bugs, the immediate goal is a higher reproduction rate, not perfection. Run the trigger 100x, parallelize, add stress, narrow timing windows, or inject sleeps. A 50% flake is debuggable; a 1% flake usually is not.

**Action:** Use the `terminal` tool to run the tight loop:

```bash
# Run a specific failing test
pytest tests/test_module.py::test_name -v

# Or run a scripted repro
python scripts/repro_bug.py

# Or run a high-repetition flaky repro
for i in {1..100}; do pytest tests/test_flake.py::test_name -q || break; done
```

### 3. Check Recent Changes

- What changed that could cause this?
- Git diff, recent commits
- New dependencies, config changes

**Action:**

```bash
# Recent commits
git log --oneline -10

# Uncommitted changes
git diff

# Changes in specific file
git log -p --follow src/problematic_file.py | head -100
```

### 4. Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems

**WHEN system has multiple components (API → service → database, CI → build → deploy):**

**BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**

For EACH component boundary:
- Log what data enters the component
- Log what data exits the component
- Verify environment/config propagation
- Check state at each layer

Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks.
THEN analyze evidence to identify the failing component.
THEN investigate that specific component.

### 5. Trace Data Flow

**WHEN error is deep in the call stack:**

- Where does the bad value originate?
- What called this function with the bad value?
- Keep tracing upstream until you find the source
- Fix at the source, not at the symptom

**Action:** Use `search_files` to trace references:

```python
# Find where the function is called
search_files("function_name(", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")

# Find where the variable is set
search_files("variable_name\\s*=", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")
```

### Phase 1 Completion Checklist

- [ ] Error messages fully read and understood
- [ ] A tight loop command exists and has been run at least once
- [ ] Loop is red-capable: it asserts the user's exact symptom, not a nearby failure
- [ ] Loop is deterministic, or a flaky bug has a high enough reproduction rate to debug
- [ ] Recent changes identified and reviewed
- [ ] Evidence gathered (logs, state, data flow)
- [ ] Problem isolated to specific component/code
- [ ] Root cause hypotheses can be stated and tested

**STOP:** Do not proceed to Phase 2 until you understand WHY it's happening.

---

## Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

### 0. Minimize the Reproduction

Once the loop is red, shrink the repro to the smallest scenario that still goes red. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut. Keep only what is load-bearing for the failure.

Done when removing any remaining element makes the loop go green. A minimal repro narrows the hypothesis space and often becomes the cleanest regression test.

### 1. Find Working Examples

- Locate similar working code in the same codebase
- What works that's similar to what's broken?

**Action:** Use `search_files` to find comparable patterns:

```python
search_files("similar_pattern", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")
```

### 2. Compare Against References

- If implementing a pattern, read the reference implementation COMPLETELY
- Don't skim — read every line
- Understand the pattern fully before applying

### 3. Identify Differences

- What's different between working and broken?
- List every difference, however small
- Don't assume "that can't matter"

### 4. Understand Dependencies

- What other components does this need?
- What settings, config, environment?
- What assumptions does it make?

---

## Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

### 1. Form Ranked Falsifiable Hypotheses

- Generate 3–5 plausible hypotheses before testing any single one.
- Rank them by likelihood and cheapness to falsify.
- State the prediction each hypothesis makes: "If X is the cause, then changing or observing Y should make Z happen."
- Discard or sharpen any hypothesis that does not make a testable prediction.

If the user is present, show the ranked list before testing. They may have domain knowledge that instantly re-ranks it. If the user is AFK, proceed with your ranking.

### 2. Test Minimally

- Test the highest-ranked hypothesis with the smallest possible probe.
- Change one variable at a time.
- Don't fix multiple things at once.
- Prefer debugger/REPL inspection when available; one breakpoint beats ten logs.
- If you add logs, tag every temporary line with a unique prefix such as `[DEBUG-a4f2]` so cleanup is a single search.

### 3. Verify Before Continuing

- Did it work? → Phase 4
- Didn't work? → Form NEW hypothesis
- DON'T add more fixes on top

### 4. When You Don't Know

- Say "I don't understand X"
- Don't pretend to know
- Ask the user for help
- Research more

---

## Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

### 1. Create Failing Test Case

- Simplest possible reproduction
- Automated test if possible
- MUST have before fixing
- Use the `test-driven-development` skill

### 2. Implement Single Fix

- Address the root cause identified
- ONE change at a time
- No "while I'm here" improvements
- No bundled refactoring

### 3. Verify Fix

```bash
# Run the specific regression test
pytest tests/test_module.py::test_regression -v

# Run full suite — no regressions
pytest tests/ -q
```

### 4. If Fix Doesn't Work — The Rule of Three

- **STOP.**
- Count: How many fixes have you tried?
- If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
- **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
- DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

### 5. If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture

**Pattern indicating an architectural problem:**
- Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling in a different place
- Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
- Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

**STOP and question fundamentals:**
- Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
- Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
- Should we refactor the architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

**Discuss with the user before attempting more fixes.**

This is NOT a failed hypothesis — this is a wrong architecture.

---

## Red Flags — STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals a new problem in a different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (Phase 4 step 5).

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question the pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence, trace data flow | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare, identify differences | Know what's different |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally, one variable at a time | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create regression test, fix root cause, verify | Bug resolved, all tests pass |

446|### ovs-db-analysis
447|1|---
448|2|name: ovs-db-analysis
449|3|description: >-
450|4|  Analyze Open vSwitch data from sosreport — conf.db, OpenFlow dumps, port stats,
451|5|  tunnels, and datapath health. Use when troubleshooting OVS packet drops, flow
452|6|  performance, bridge/port/interface issues, DPDK vs kernel datapath, or when the
453|7|  user mentions sosreport openvswitch, ovs-ofctl, ovsdb-tool, or ovs-db-analysis.
454|8|---
455|9|
456|10|# OVS Database and Flow Analysis
457|11|
458|12|This skill provides detailed analysis of Open vSwitch (OVS) data collected via sosreport. It operates in four modes:
459|13|
460|14|1. **Default mode**: Full analysis - conf.db + all text files (requires ovsdb-tool, falls back to text files if not available)
461|15|2. **Database mode (`--db`)**: Database only - analyze conf.db (requires ovsdb-tool)
462|16|3. **Text files mode (`--flows-only`)**: Text files only - no ovsdb-tool needed
463|17|4. **Query mode (`--query`)**: Run custom OVSDB JSON queries (requires ovsdb-tool)
464|18|
465|19|## When to Use This Skill
466|20|
467|21|Use this skill when:
468|22|- **Troubleshooting packet drops** - Find drop flows being hit
469|23|- **Analyzing flow performance** - View top flows by packet count
470|24|- Analyzing OVS configuration from a sosreport
471|25|- Troubleshooting bridge, port, or interface issues
472|26|- Investigating DPDK vs kernelspace datapath
473|27|- Reviewing tunnel configurations (VXLAN, Geneve, GRE)
474|28|- Checking port statistics (drops, errors, traffic)
475|29|- Mapping Kubernetes pods to OVS interfaces
476|30|
477|31|## Prerequisites
478|32|
479|33|**Default mode** (full analysis):
480|34|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
481|35|- Falls back to `--flows-only` if ovsdb-tool not found
482|36|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory and `conf.db`
483|37|
484|38|**Database mode** (`--db`):
485|39|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
486|40|  - Check: `which ovsdb-tool`
487|41|  - Fedora/RHEL: `sudo dnf install openvswitch`
488|42|  - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install openvswitch-common`
489|43|- Sosreport with `conf.db` file
490|44|
491|45|**Text files mode** (`--flows-only`):
492|46|- No special tools needed - works out of the box!
493|47|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory
494|48|
495|49|**Query mode** (`--query`):
496|50|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed
497|51|- Incompatible with `--flows-only`
498|52|
499|53|## File Locations in Sosreport
500|54|
501|55|The sosreport collects:
502|56|```
503|57|sosreport-hostname-date/
504|58|├── etc/openvswitch/conf.db              (OVS database - for --db mode)
505|59|├── var/lib/openvswitch/conf.db          (alternate location)
506|60|└── sos_commands/openvswitch/            (default mode uses these)
507|61|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show              (topology)
508|62|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge       (bridge details)
509|63|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface    (interface details)
510|64|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch (system info)
511|65|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_<bridge>    (OpenFlow entries)
512|66|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_<bridge>    (Port statistics)
513|67|    ├── ovs-appctl_coverage.show         (internal stats)
514|68|    ├── ovs-appctl_upcall.show           (datapath health)
515|69|    ├── ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v     (tunnel ports)
516|70|    └── ...
517|71|```
518|72|
519|73|## Analysis Script
520|74|
521|75|The analysis script is located at:
522|76|```
523|77|<plugin-root>/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/analyze_ovs_db.py
524|78|```
525|79|
526|80|## Implementation Steps
527|81|
528|82|### Step 1: Locate the Analysis Script
529|83|
530|84|```bash
531|85|SCRIPT_PATH=$(find ~ -name "analyze_ovs_db.py" -path "*/sosreport/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/*" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
532|86|
533|87|if [ -z "$SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then
534|88|    echo "ERROR: analyze_ovs_db.py script not found."
535|89|    exit 1
536|90|fi
537|91|```
538|92|
539|93|### Step 2: Run the Analysis
540|94|
541|95|```bash
542|96|# Default: Full analysis - conf.db + text files (requires ovsdb-tool)
543|97|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date/
544|98|
545|99|# Analyze from archive
546|100|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date.tar.xz
547|101|
548|102|# Database only mode (requires ovsdb-tool)
549|103|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --db
550|104|
551|105|# Text files only mode (no ovsdb-tool needed)
552|106|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --flows-only
553|107|```
554|108|
555|109|### Step 3: Custom Queries (Optional, requires --db)
556|110|
557|111|For specific investigations, use raw OVSDB queries:
558|112|
559|113|```bash
560|114|# Query all bridges
561|115|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Bridge", "where":[], "columns":["name","datapath_type","fail_mode"]}]'
562|116|
563|117|# Query VXLAN interfaces
564|118|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[["type","==","vxlan"]], "columns":["name","options"]}]'
565|119|
566|120|# Query interfaces with errors
567|121|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[], "columns":["name","error"]}]'
568|122|```

570|124|## Analysis Output
571|125|
572|126|The default mode analyzes:
573|127|
574|128|| Analysis | Source File | Description |
575|129||----------|-------------|-------------|
576|130|| System Info | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch` | OVS/DPDK version, system type, external IDs |
577|131|| Topology | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show` | Bridge overview with ports grouped by type |
578|132|| Bridge Details | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge` | Datapath type, fail mode, CT zones |
579|133|| Interfaces | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface` | By type, pod interfaces with mapping |
580|134|| OpenFlow | `ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_*` | Flow counts, drops, top flows |
581|135|| Port Stats | `ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_*` | RX/TX drops and errors |
582|136|| Tunnels | `ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v` | Configured tunnel ports |
583|137|| Datapath Health | `ovs-appctl_upcall.show` | Flow table usage vs limit |
584|138|| OVS Stats | `ovs-appctl_coverage.show` | Internal counters (netlink, OVSDB, etc.) |
585|139|
586|140|## OpenFlow Analysis Features
587|141|
588|142|| Feature | Description |
589|143||---------|-------------|
590|144|| Flow Count | Total flows per bridge (total, drop, with hits) |
591|145|| Drop Detection | Flows with `actions=drop` that have packet hits |
592|146|| Top Flows | Most active flows sorted by n_packets |
593|147|| Table Distribution | Flow counts per OpenFlow table |

598|152|
599|153|## OVN Internal Tables (Ignore Drops in These)
600|154|
601|155|When analyzing drop flows in OVN-managed bridges (br-int), **ignore drops in table 44 and tables 64-87** as these are internal OVN mechanics, not security policy or real packet drops.
602|156|
603|157|> **⚠️ Note:** OVN and OVS are complex systems and table mappings can change between releases. Always verify drop analysis against the specific OVN version in use. When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release.
604|158|
605|159|| Table | Name | Purpose |
606|160||-------|------|---------|
607|161|| **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** |
608|162|| 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later |
609|163|| 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping |
610|164|| 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups |
611|165|| 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups |
612|166|| 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks |
613|167|| 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin |
614|168|| 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups |
615|169|| 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security |
616|170|| 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security |
617|171|| 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling |
618|172|| 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity |
619|173|| **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** |
620|174|| 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup |
621|175|| 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading |
622|176|| 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding |
623|177|| 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save |
624|178|| 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading |
625|179|| 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup |
626|180|
627|181|**Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:**
628|182|- **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`)
629|183|- **Table 0**: Initial classification drops
630|184|- **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops

632|186|## Common Analysis Scenarios

757|### kernel-fuse-diagnosis
758|1|---
759|2|name: kernel-fuse-diagnosis
760|3|description: >
761|4|  FUSE（用户态文件系统）内核端故障诊断技能。当用户提到 FUSE 文件系统 hang、
762|5|  所有操作返回 EIO、FUSE daemon 崩溃/重启、请求队列阻塞、D 状态进程堆积、
763|6|  /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 异常、libfuse 兼容性、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
764|7|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 FUSE daemon 死锁、容器中 /dev/fuse 权限问题、
765|8|  FUSE 性能退化等关键词时，必须使用本技能。
766|9|  覆盖场景：FUSE daemon 崩溃后 EIO、请求队列阻塞与 D 状态、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
767|10|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 daemon 死锁、/dev/fuse 权限问题、内核 FUSE 模块 Bug、
768|11|  混合复杂 FUSE 故障。即使只收到"文件系统挂了"、"目录打不开"、"ls 卡死"但挂载点
769|12|  为 FUSE 类型时也应触发本技能。
770|13|  支持 FUSE 全链路诊断（sysfs 队列 → 内核参数 → daemon 进程 → 代码级根因）。
771|14|---
772|15|
773|16|# FUSE 内核端故障诊断（三层下钻：系统层 → 类型层 → 代码根因层）
774|17|
775|18|## 第一节：故障目录结构
776|19|
777|20|```text
778|21|fuse_case/                  # 故障案例目录
779|22|├── scripts/                # 【内置】本技能的诊断脚本
780|23|│   ├── 01_baseline_info.sh
781|24|│   ├── branch_A_daemon_crash.sh
782|25|│   ├── branch_B_req_queue.sh
783|26|│   ├── branch_C_max_read_write.sh
784|27|│   ├── branch_D_writeback_cache.sh

787|30|│   ├── branch_G_kernel_bug.sh
788|31|│   └── branch_H_mixed.sh

804|47|---
805|48|
806|49|## 第二节：分析策略（三层下钻，逐层收敛）
807|50|
808|51|FUSE 内核端故障诊断采用**三层下钻模型**，从最外层逐层深入，层间存在依赖关系：
809|52|
810|53|```
811|54|┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
812|55|│                   三层下钻分析模型                                 │
813|56|│                                                                 │
814|57|│   L1: 系统层         mount -t fuse /proc/mounts                 │
815|58|│       │               /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*                │
816|59|│       └─ 判断：FUSE 挂载点是否正常？连接是否存在？               │
817|60|│                                                                 │
818|61|│   L2: 类型层         strace -p <daemon_pid>                     │
819|62|│       │               cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting     │
820|63|│       └─ 判断：是 EIO？请求阻塞？性能退化？权限问题？            │
821|64|│                                                                 │
822|65|│   L3: 代码/内核层    FUSE daemon 源码分析                       │
823|66|│                      内核 FUSE 模块参数 (/sys/module/fuse/)     │
824|67|│                      /dev/fuse 设备状态                          │
825|68|│                      └─ 根因定位：daemon 崩溃 / 队列阻塞 / 配置  │
826|69|│                                                                 │
827|70|│   每层输出：证据 + 结论。L3 输出最终根因。                       │
828|71|└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
829|72|```

831|74|### 故障分类树
832|75|
833|76|```
834|77|L1 ─ FUSE 挂载点与连接检查
835|78|│
836|79|├─ L2 ─ 挂载点正常？─────── 否 ──→ 非 FUSE 问题，转其他技能
837|80|│                         是
838|81|│                         ↓
839|82|├─ L2 ─ 操作返回 EIO？──── 是 ──→ Branch A (Daemon Crash)
840|83|│                         否
